s: Article 21A of the Constitution provides for free and compulsory education to children in which age group?
x: Article 21A guarantees free and compulsory education to all children from 6 to 14 years of age.
tq: Use the precise constitutional age range to distinguish Article 21A from Articles 45 and 51A(k).
sec: Right to Education - Article 21A, inserting amendment and commencement, RTE Act 2009, earlier cases  [APPSC]

s: Article 21A was inserted into the Constitution by which Constitutional Amendment Act?
x: The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A.
tq: Split the amendment-number and year combination from nearby constitutional amendments.
sec: Right to Education - Article 21A, inserting amendment and commencement, RTE Act 2009, earlier cases  [APPSC]

s: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009, along with Article 21A, came into force on:
x: The RTE Act, 2009 and Article 21A came into force on 1 April 2010.
tq: Discriminate between the enactment year and the commencement date.
sec: Right to Education - Article 21A, inserting amendment and commencement, RTE Act 2009, earlier cases  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Right to Education Act, 2009:
1. It provides for 25 per cent entry-level seats in unaided private schools for children belonging to weaker groups.
2. The 25 per cent provision applies to minority schools without exception.
3. The Act has been amended in 2012, 2017, 2019 and 2022.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: The Act provides 25 per cent entry-level seats in unaided private schools for weaker groups, but the provision does not apply to minority schools. It was amended in 2012, 2017, 2019 and 2022.
tq: Find the wrong statement by testing the absolute claim about minority schools.
sec: Right to Education - Article 21A, inserting amendment and commencement, RTE Act 2009, earlier cases  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Article 21A — Early childhood care below six years
Article 45 — Free and compulsory education from six to fourteen years
Article 51A(k) — Duty of parent or guardian to provide educational opportunities to a child or ward aged six to fourteen years
Article 21 — Reservation of entry-level seats in private schools
x: Article 51A(k) imposes the duty on a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to a child or ward between 6 and 14 years. Article 21A concerns that age group as a Fundamental Right, while Article 45 concerns early childhood care below six years.
tq: Match each constitutional provision with its correct subject and age group.
sec: Right to Education - Article 21A, inserting amendment and commencement, RTE Act 2009, earlier cases  [APPSC]

s:
With reference to the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, consider the following statements:
1. It inserted Article 21A.
2. It modified Article 45 to concern early childhood care and education below six years.
3. It inserted Article 51A(k) relating to the educational opportunities of children aged 6 to 14 years.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: The 86th Amendment made all three changes: it inserted Article 21A, changed Article 45 and added the parental duty under Article 51A(k).
tq: Recognise the common amendment behind three related constitutional provisions.
sec: Right to Education - Article 21A, inserting amendment and commencement, RTE Act 2009, earlier cases  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following is NOT a Fundamental Right under Article 21A?
o: Free elementary education for children aged 6 to 14 years
Education in the manner determined by the State
Free higher education for all citizens
Compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 years
x: Article 21A covers only free and compulsory elementary education for children aged 6 to 14 years. Higher and professional education are not Fundamental Rights under Article 21A.
tq: Identify the excluded level of education rather than being distracted by the constitutional wording.
sec: Right to Education - Article 21A, inserting amendment and commencement, RTE Act 2009, earlier cases  [APPSC]

s: The phrase “in such manner as the State may determine” in Article 21A indicates that:
o: The right applies only when the State has sufficient financial resources
The State may decide whether education is a Fundamental Right
The State may decide the manner of providing free and compulsory education
Only local bodies may provide elementary education
x: Article 21A makes education a Fundamental Right while leaving the manner of its provision to be determined by the State.
tq: Separate the existence of a Fundamental Right from the manner in which it is implemented.
sec: Right to Education - Article 21A, inserting amendment and commencement, RTE Act 2009, earlier cases  [APPSC]

s: Section 3 of the Right to Education Act, 2009, principally provides that:
o: The State may replace elementary education with vocational training for all children
Every child aged 6 to 14 years has a right to free and compulsory education in a neighbourhood school until completion of elementary education
Only children admitted to minority schools are entitled to free education
Every adult has a right to free professional education in any State institution
x: Section 3 gives every child aged 6 to 14 years the right to free and compulsory education in a neighbourhood school until elementary education is completed.
tq: Recall the operative provision by identifying its beneficiary, age group, institution and educational level.
sec: Right to Education - Article 21A, inserting amendment and commencement, RTE Act 2009, earlier cases  [APPSC]

s: Under the Right to Education Act, 2009, schools are reimbursed on the basis of:
o: The total number of teachers appointed
The number of children completing secondary education
The annual income of the school management
x: Schools covered by the RTE framework are reimbursed on the basis of per-child expenditure.
tq: Test the exact basis of reimbursement rather than the broader objective of the Act.
sec: Right to Education - Article 21A, inserting amendment and commencement, RTE Act 2009, earlier cases  [APPSC]

s: Which institutions are associated with review and redress of grievances under the Right to Education framework?
o: Election Commission and State Election Commissions
UPSC and State Public Service Commissions
Finance Commission and State Finance Commissions
x: The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights and State Commissions for Protection of Child Rights review and address grievances under the framework. Their statutory basis is associated with the CPCR Act, 2005.
tq: Use the institutional-function association to eliminate bodies with unrelated constitutional roles.
sec: Right to Education - Article 21A, inserting amendment and commencement, RTE Act 2009, earlier cases  [APPSC]

s:
Arrange the following developments relating to the right to education in chronological order:
A. Unnikrishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh
B. Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka
C. 86th Constitutional Amendment Act
D. Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act
x: Mohini Jain was decided in 1992, Unnikrishnan in 1993, the 86th Amendment was enacted in 2002, and the RTE Act was enacted in 2009.
tq: Fix the sequence using the dated judicial decisions followed by the amendment and enabling legislation.
sec: Right to Education - Article 21A, inserting amendment and commencement, RTE Act 2009, earlier cases  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding important cases on the right to education:
1. Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka was decided in 1992.
2. Mohini Jain held that the right to education flows from Article 21.
3. Unnikrishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh held that free education is available only up to 14 years, with education beyond that depending on the State’s economic capacity.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All three statements correctly describe the years and rulings in Mohini Jain and Unnikrishnan. These decisions preceded the constitutional insertion of Article 21A.
tq: Combine the year, case name and holding, checking each statement independently.
sec: Right to Education - Article 21A, inserting amendment and commencement, RTE Act 2009, earlier cases  [APPSC]

s: The constitutional status of the Right to Education is best described as follows:
o: It is a Fundamental Duty of parents alone
It is only a Directive Principle of State Policy
It is a statutory right unrelated to Article 21
It is a Fundamental Right and is treated as an extension of the right to life
x: The Right to Education is a Fundamental Right under Article 21A and is treated as an extension of the right to life under Article 21.
tq: Distinguish the Fundamental Right from the related Directive Principle and parental Fundamental Duty.
sec: Right to Education - Article 21A, inserting amendment and commencement, RTE Act 2009, earlier cases  [APPSC]

s: The right to privacy was declared to be intrinsic to life and personal liberty under Article 21 in:
o: Gobind v. State of Madhya Pradesh
Kharak Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh
K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
x: In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, decided in 2017, the Supreme Court held that privacy is intrinsic to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and protected under Part III.
tq: Identify the authoritative later case rather than the earlier cases that only raised or partially recognised privacy concerns.
sec: Right to privacy - article, Puttaswamy bench, cases overruled, tests  [APPSC]

s: The judgment in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India was delivered on:
x: The Puttaswamy privacy judgment was delivered on 24 August 2017.
tq: Distinguish the exact judgment date from nearby constitutional and subsequent privacy-law dates.
sec: Right to privacy - article, Puttaswamy bench, cases overruled, tests  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the bench and conclusion in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India?
o: A nine-judge bench unanimously recognised privacy as intrinsic to life and personal liberty
A seven-judge bench unanimously held that privacy is outside Part III
A five-judge bench by a majority held that privacy is only a statutory right
A nine-judge bench held that privacy is available only to citizens
x: A unanimous nine-judge bench recognised privacy as intrinsic to life and personal liberty and protected under Article 21 and Part III.
tq: Check the bench strength, unanimity and constitutional status together.
sec: Right to privacy - article, Puttaswamy bench, cases overruled, tests  [APPSC]

s: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India overruled M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh to the extent that those decisions:
o: Recognised proportionality as the sole test for all restrictions
Denied the existence of privacy as a protected constitutional interest
Declared education to be a Directive Principle
x: Puttaswamy overruled M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) insofar as they denied privacy as a constitutional protection.
tq: Focus on the limited extent of overruling instead of treating the earlier judgments as wholly erased.
sec: Right to privacy - article, Puttaswamy bench, cases overruled, tests  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched in relation to the evolution of the right to privacy?
o: M.P. Sharma — 2017 recognition of privacy as intrinsic to Article 21
Kharak Singh — early concern relating to privacy
Gobind — denial that privacy forms part of liberty
Puttaswamy — privacy limited to a statutory entitlement
x: Kharak Singh represents an early concern relating to privacy. Gobind v. State of Madhya Pradesh in 1975 recognised privacy as part of liberty, while Puttaswamy gave privacy comprehensive constitutional protection.
tq: Use the chronological development of the doctrine to separate early concern, partial recognition and final constitutional affirmation.
sec: Right to privacy - article, Puttaswamy bench, cases overruled, tests  [APPSC]

s:
For an intrusion into the right to privacy to withstand constitutional scrutiny, which of the following requirements are relevant?
1. Legality, meaning the existence of a law.
2. A legitimate aim or need.
3. Proportionality.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: The privacy restriction framework includes legality, legitimate aim or need and proportionality. All three requirements are relevant to assessing an intrusion.
tq: Recognise the cumulative constitutional test instead of selecting only the most familiar element.
sec: Right to privacy - article, Puttaswamy bench, cases overruled, tests  [APPSC]

s: A government measure restricts personal data without any supporting law, although it claims to pursue a public objective. Which requirement of the privacy test is most clearly absent?
x: The legality requirement demands that an intrusion into privacy be supported by a law. A claimed public objective cannot substitute for the existence of legal authority.
tq: Apply the first step of the privacy test by asking whether the restriction has a legal basis.
sec: Right to privacy - article, Puttaswamy bench, cases overruled, tests  [APPSC]

s: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is associated with which institution?
x: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 provides for a Data Protection Board. The enacted law is an Act, not merely a Personal Data Protection Bill.
tq: Discriminate between the enacted statute and the earlier bill terminology, and identify its associated body.
sec: Right to privacy - article, Puttaswamy bench, cases overruled, tests  [APPSC]

s: The proportionality requirement in privacy jurisprudence was subsequently applied in the context of Aadhaar in:
x: The proportionality framework developed in privacy jurisprudence was subsequently applied to Aadhaar in 2018.
tq: Separate the year of the Puttaswamy judgment from the year of its later application to Aadhaar.
sec: Right to privacy - article, Puttaswamy bench, cases overruled, tests  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following cases recognised the right to travel abroad as a facet of Article 21?
o: Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar
Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar
x: Maneka Gandhi (1978) recognised the right to travel abroad under Article 21. Satwant Singh Sawhney (1967) had earlier dealt with the same right.
tq: Direct case-to-right recall using closely related Article 21 cases as distractors.
sec: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

s: The right to marry a person of one’s choice was recognised in which of the following cases?
o: Common Cause v. Union of India
Supriyo Chakraborty v. Union of India
Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka
x: Shafin Jahan, popularly associated with the Hadiya case, recognised the individual’s choice of partner under Article 21 in 2018.
tq: Confusable-case discrimination between marriage, privacy and euthanasia decisions.
sec: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

s: With reference to rights read into Article 21, which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Free legal aid — Subhash Kumar case
Emergency medical care — Maneka Gandhi case
x: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985) recognised livelihood as a component of the right to life. The other cases are associated with speedy trial, clean environment and travel abroad respectively.
tq: Start from the sure case-right pair and eliminate swapped authorities.
sec: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding rights recognised under Article 21:
1. Hussainara Khatoon recognised speedy trial as a component of Article 21.
2. Subhash Kumar recognised the right to a clean environment.
3. Chameli Singh recognised the right to shelter.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All three statements are correct. Hussainara Khatoon dealt with speedy trial, Subhash Kumar with a clean environment, and Chameli Singh with shelter.
tq: Statement-combination question requiring separate case-right identification.
sec: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

s: The right to emergency medical care under Article 21 was recognised in which case?
o: M.H. Hoskot v. State of Maharashtra
K.A. Najeeb v. Union of India
Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity v. State of West Bengal
x: Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity (1996) recognised the obligation to provide emergency medical care as part of Article 21.
tq: Direct case recall with distractors drawn from other Article 21 rights.
sec: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

s: M.H. Hoskot v. State of Maharashtra is associated with which of the following rights under Article 21?
o: Right to marry a person of choice
x: M.H. Hoskot (1978) is associated with free legal aid as a component of fair procedure and personal liberty.
tq: One-fact case association using nearby Article 21 doctrines as distractors.
sec: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Common Cause — Right to marry as an unqualified fundamental right
K.A. Najeeb — Reaffirmation of speedy trial
x: Common Cause (2018) recognised the right to die with dignity and the validity of living wills. Supriyo Chakraborty (2023) held that there is no unqualified fundamental right to marry as such.
tq: Find the wrong case-holding pair, especially the swapped marriage and euthanasia doctrines.
sec: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

s: In which case did the Supreme Court recognise the right to privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21?
o: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
x: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) recognised privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21.
tq: Direct identification of the landmark privacy case.
sec: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following statements correctly describes the effect of the Supriyo Chakraborty judgment of 2023?
o: It recognised an unqualified fundamental right to marry for all persons.
It declared the right to privacy unconstitutional.
It held that travel abroad is not protected under Article 21.
It held that there is no fundamental right to marry as such, while other Article 21 rights remain recognised.
x: Supriyo Chakraborty held that there is no unqualified fundamental right to marry as such. This does not remove Article 21 protection for dignity, privacy or choice of partner.
tq: Discriminate between the right to choose a partner and an unqualified right to marry.
sec: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements about Article 21:
1. It is available to both citizens and non-citizens.
2. It has been interpreted to include dignity, health and mental health.
3. It includes protection against solitary confinement and compensation for violation of rights.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Article 21 protects citizens and non-citizens and has been expansively interpreted to include dignity, health, mental health, protection against solitary confinement and compensation for violations.
tq: Cumulative statement testing of the expanding scope of a constitutional right.
sec: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

s: Which case recognised the right to walk safely on footpaths by invoking Articles 19(1)(d) and 21 and referred to restitutionary remedies?
o: Chameli Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh
M.H. Hoskot v. State of Maharashtra
Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity v. State of West Bengal
x: Maniyar Iliyaz v. P. Ayyappan (2026) connected safe walking on footpaths with Articles 19(1)(d) and 21 and referred to restitutionary remedies.
tq: Current judicial-development recall with precise constitutional provisions.
sec: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

s: Article 20(1) primarily protects a person against which of the following?
o: Ex post facto criminal law imposing conviction or a heavier penalty
Retrospective application of every civil law
x: Article 20(1) prohibits conviction under a criminal law that was not in force when the act was committed and prohibits a heavier penalty than the one applicable at that time.
tq: Direct clause-to-protection recall, distinguishing criminal from civil consequences.
sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 20(1):
1. It applies to criminal laws.
2. It prohibits a heavier penalty than the penalty applicable when the offence was committed.
3. It bars the conduct of a trial itself in every case involving a later-enacted criminal law.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Article 20(1) bars conviction and a greater penalty, but it does not necessarily bar the trial itself.
tq: Test the precise scope of a protection rather than its broad slogan.
sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

s: The protection against double jeopardy under Article 20(2) means that a person shall not be:
o: Prosecuted and punished more than once for the same offence
Subjected to both civil and criminal proceedings
Arrested and questioned twice for any purpose
x: Article 20(2) protects against being prosecuted and punished twice for the same offence. Its constitutional scope concerns prosecution and punishment by a court or judicial tribunal.
tq: Exact-word discrimination between prosecution, punishment and other proceedings.
sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following is outside the constitutional protection against double jeopardy under Article 20(2), as stated in the recognised scope of the provision?
o: A second judicial punishment for the same offence
Prosecution and punishment by a court
x: Article 20(2) covers prosecution and punishment by a court or judicial tribunal, but it does not extend to departmental proceedings.
tq: Identify the exception by distinguishing judicial punishment from departmental action.
sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

s:
With reference to Article 20(3), consider the following statements:
1. It applies to criminal proceedings.
2. It covers oral and documentary testimony.
3. It generally treats fingerprints and physical specimens as testimonial self-incrimination.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Physical evidence such as fingerprints is not treated as testimonial compulsion under Article 20(3), as recognised in Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961).
tq: Separate testimonial evidence from physical evidence before selecting the combination.
sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following forms of evidence was held not to be covered by the protection against self-incrimination in Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961)?
o: A compelled written statement describing the offence
x: Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961) distinguished physical evidence such as fingerprints from testimonial compulsion protected by Article 20(3).
tq: Confusable-pair discrimination between physical evidence and testimony.
sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

s: In Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010), the Supreme Court held that which of the following, when conducted without consent, violates Article 20(3)?
o: Verification of age through official records
x: Selvi (2010) held that narco-analysis, polygraph examination and brain-mapping without consent violate the protection against testimonial compulsion under Article 20(3).
tq: Direct case-to-doctrine recall using physical-evidence distractors.
sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following correctly describes the applicability of Article 20?
o: It is available only during an Emergency.
It is available only to Indian citizens.
It is available to citizens, foreigners and legal persons such as companies.
It is available only to natural persons present in India.
x: The protections under Article 20 are available to citizens, foreigners and legal persons such as companies, subject to the nature of the particular protection.
tq: Membership and coverage trap involving citizens, aliens and companies.
sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following is NOT covered by Article 20 protections?
o: Double prosecution and punishment for the same offence
x: Article 20 does not cover retrospective civil or tax laws. Article 20(1) is confined to ex post facto criminal laws.
tq: Find the excluded category by separating criminal law from civil and tax law.
sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

s: Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, the provision corresponding to the protection against double jeopardy is contained in:
x: Section 337 of the BNSS contains the provision relating to double jeopardy; it corresponds to the earlier Section 300 of the CrPC.
tq: Section-number discrimination between the new code and the repealed CrPC provision.
sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

s: The protections under Article 20 are regarded as non-suspendable during an Emergency. Which of the following best reflects this position?
o: Article 20 protections may be suspended by executive order alone.
Article 20 applies only after the Emergency is withdrawn.
Article 20 protects only citizens during an Emergency.
Article 20 protections continue even during an Emergency.
x: The protections guaranteed by Article 20 are non-suspendable during an Emergency. They are not confined to citizens alone.
tq: Apply the constitutional protection to an Emergency situation without confusing it with ordinary restrictions.
sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

s:
Arrange the following cases in chronological order:
A. Common Cause
B. P. Rathinam
C. Gian Kaur
D. Aruna Shanbaug
x: P. Rathinam was decided in 1994, Gian Kaur in 1996, Aruna Shanbaug in 2011 and Common Cause in 2018.
tq: Use the earliest and latest cases first, then place the two intervening rulings.
sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

s: What was the ruling in P. Rathinam (1994)?
o: A fundamental right to marry was recognised.
Passive euthanasia was permitted under High Court supervision.
Section 309 IPC was upheld without qualification.
Section 309 IPC, dealing with attempted suicide, was held unconstitutional.
x: P. Rathinam (1994) held Section 309 IPC unconstitutional and treated suicide as something that should not be criminally punished.
tq: Direct case-holding recall with nearby euthanasia rulings as distractors.
sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

s: Which case overruled the decision in P. Rathinam and held that there is no right to die, while recognising a right to die with dignity?
x: Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab (1996) overruled P. Rathinam. It held that there is no right to death but recognised the right to die with dignity and upheld Section 309 IPC.
tq: Identify the overruling case by separating right to die from right to die with dignity.
sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements about the right to die and euthanasia cases:
1. Maruti Shripati Dubal held that the right to die formed part of Article 21.
2. Gian Kaur overruled the position in Maruti Shripati Dubal and P. Rathinam.
3. Common Cause recognised the right to die with dignity as a fundamental right under Article 21.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Gian Kaur overruled P. Rathinam, but the material does not state that it overruled Maruti Shripati Dubal in the same formulation; the Bombay High Court decision preceded Rathinam.
tq: Avoid overextending an overruling judgment beyond the specific case identified.
sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following correctly describes the decision in Aruna Shanbaug (2011)?
o: The euthanasia plea was rejected, but passive euthanasia was allowed under strict conditions and High Court supervision.
A living will was declared invalid in every circumstance.
Active euthanasia was made a general fundamental right.
x: In Aruna Shanbaug (2011), the plea was rejected, but passive euthanasia was permitted under strict conditions and High Court supervision.
tq: Distinguish passive euthanasia from active euthanasia and from the later living-will ruling.
sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

s: The validity of a living will or advance directive in the context of the right to die with dignity was recognised in:
x: Common Cause (2018) recognised the right to die with dignity as part of Article 21 and upheld the validity of a living will or advance directive.
tq: Direct identification of the latest landmark holding in a sequence of related cases.
sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

s: With regard to attempted suicide in India, which of the following statements is correct?
o: The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 created a general offence of attempted suicide.
The BNS decriminalised every act intended to compel a public servant.
The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 decriminalised attempted suicide in effect, and the BNS has no general offence of attempted suicide.
The BNS retained Section 309 IPC unchanged as a general offence.
x: The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 decriminalised attempted suicide in effect. The BNS, in force from 1 July 2024, contains no general offence of attempted suicide.
tq: Compare the position under the Mental Healthcare Act and the post-IPC BNS framework.
sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

s: Under Section 226 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, an attempt to commit suicide is punishable when it is made for the purpose of:
o: Compelling or restraining a public servant from discharging official duties
x: Section 226 BNS applies only to an attempt to compel or restrain a public servant from exercising lawful powers or discharging official duties; it is not a general offence of attempted suicide.
tq: Apply the narrow statutory exception instead of treating it as a general prohibition.
sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

s: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 replaced the Indian Penal Code with effect from:
x: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 came into force on 1 July 2024. It does not retain a general offence of attempted suicide corresponding to Section 309 IPC.
tq: Date-based recall of the transition from IPC to BNS.
sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following best distinguishes ‘procedure established by law’ from ‘due process of law’ in the context of Article 21?
o: The former examines the fairness of law, whereas the latter examines only legislative enactment
The former requires a procedure enacted by the legislature, whereas the latter also examines whether the procedure is fair and reasonable
The former applies only to preventive detention, whereas the latter applies only to civil rights
Both expressions have exactly the same meaning in Indian constitutional law
x: ‘Procedure established by law’ requires compliance with a law enacted by the legislature. ‘Due process of law’ additionally requires the law and procedure to satisfy standards of fairness and reasonableness.
tq: Discriminate between two closely related constitutional expressions by identifying the additional fairness test.
sec: Procedure established by law vs due process - A.K. Gopalan, Maneka Gandhi

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the A.K. Gopalan case:
1. It was decided in 1950.
2. It held that Article 21 protected an individual only against executive action.
3. It accepted that courts could examine the reasonableness of every law affecting personal liberty.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: The A.K. Gopalan decision was delivered in 1950 and treated Article 21 as protection mainly against executive action. It did not permit courts to examine the reasonableness of the law in the later Maneka Gandhi sense.
tq: Find the statement that reverses the limited approach adopted in the earlier case.
sec: Procedure established by law vs due process - A.K. Gopalan, Maneka Gandhi

s: Which of the following correctly describes the constitutional position after Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)?
o: Article 21 was confined exclusively to executive action
The Court rejected all elements of due process from Article 21
The procedure affecting life or personal liberty must be fair, just and reasonable
Articles 14, 19 and 21 were treated as completely independent of one another
x: The Maneka Gandhi decision held that a procedure affecting life or personal liberty must be fair, just and reasonable and must not be arbitrary.
tq: Identify the precise judicial test introduced by the later landmark judgment.
sec: Procedure established by law vs due process - A.K. Gopalan, Maneka Gandhi

s: The expression ‘golden triangle’ of fundamental rights refers to the interrelationship among which Articles?
x: Maneka Gandhi established a close relationship among Articles 14, 19 and 21, commonly described as the golden triangle of fundamental rights.
tq: Recall the standard constitutional grouping associated with the Maneka Gandhi doctrine.
sec: Procedure established by law vs due process - A.K. Gopalan, Maneka Gandhi

s: Which one of the following is a major difference between the A.K. Gopalan and Maneka Gandhi approaches to Article 21?
o: A.K. Gopalan introduced American due process, whereas Maneka Gandhi restored the Japanese approach
A.K. Gopalan excluded legislative action from scrutiny under Article 21, whereas Maneka Gandhi extended protection against arbitrary legislation
A.K. Gopalan linked Articles 14, 19 and 21, whereas Maneka Gandhi separated them
A.K. Gopalan dealt with preventive detention, whereas Maneka Gandhi dealt only with property rights
x: A.K. Gopalan treated Article 21 narrowly and did not subject legislation to the later fairness review. Maneka Gandhi held that Article 21 also protects against arbitrary legislative action.
tq: Compare the two cases across the exact dimensions of legislative scrutiny and Article 21 protection.
sec: Procedure established by law vs due process - A.K. Gopalan, Maneka Gandhi

s:
Under Article 22(1) and Article 22(2), a person subjected to an ordinary arrest has which of the following rights?
1. To be informed of the grounds of arrest
2. To consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of choice
3. To be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours, excluding journey time
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Article 22(1) and 22(2) provide all three safeguards in the case of an ordinary arrest: information about the grounds, legal representation, and production before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours excluding journey time.
tq: Check the complete constitutional package of safeguards rather than selecting only one arrest right.

s: The safeguards under Article 22(1) and Article 22(2) are not available to which of the following persons under Article 22(3)?
o: A person produced before a magistrate within 24 hours
An enemy alien and a person detained under a preventive detention law
A person arrested under an ordinary warrant
Every person arrested for a criminal offence
x: Article 22(3) excludes an enemy alien and a person detained under a preventive detention law from the safeguards in Article 22(1) and 22(2).
tq: Use the constitutional exceptions to ordinary-arrest safeguards as the decisive pair.
sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

s: Which of the following is NOT covered by the ordinary-arrest safeguards under Article 22(1) and Article 22(2)?
x: The listed situations—arrest under court orders, civil arrest and deportation of aliens—are not covered by the ordinary-arrest safeguards under Article 22(1) and 22(2).

s: Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which provisions correspond broadly to the earlier CrPC provisions concerning communication of grounds of arrest and production before a magistrate?
o: Sections 47 and 58; earlier Sections 50 and 57 of the CrPC
Sections 50 and 57; earlier Sections 47 and 58 of the CrPC
Sections 22 and 24; earlier Sections 20 and 21 of the CrPC
Sections 58 and 60; earlier Sections 47 and 50 of the CrPC
x: Sections 47 and 58 of the BNSS correspond broadly to the earlier CrPC Sections 50 and 57 concerning the relevant arrest safeguards.
tq: Discriminate between present BNSS section numbers and their earlier CrPC counterparts.

s: Which one of the following best describes preventive detention?
o: Detention based on suspicion of future acts and imposed without a criminal trial
Detention exclusively for non-payment of a civil debt
Detention after conviction for the purpose of executing a sentence
Detention ordered only by a criminal court after a finding of guilt
x: Preventive detention is detention without trial based on the apprehension that a person may commit specified harmful acts in the future. Punitive detention follows conviction.
tq: Separate preventive detention from punitive detention by focusing on timing and purpose.

s: A person detained under a preventive detention law may ordinarily be detained beyond three months only when:
o: An Advisory Board reports sufficient cause for continued detention
The President personally reviews the detention
The detainee waives the right of representation
The police commissioner grants written permission
x: Article 22(4) requires an Advisory Board, consisting of High Court judges or persons qualified to be High Court judges, to report sufficient cause before preventive detention continues beyond three months.
tq: Ask which constitutional authority supplies the mandatory safeguard for extended preventive detention.
sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

s:
Consider the following statements regarding preventive detention under Article 22:
1. The grounds of detention must be communicated to the detainee.
2. The detainee must be given the earliest opportunity to make a representation against the order.
3. Parliament may prescribe the maximum period for which a person may be detained under a preventive detention law.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Article 22(5) requires communication of grounds and the earliest opportunity for representation. Article 22(7) permits Parliament to prescribe the maximum period of preventive detention in the circumstances specified by the Constitution.
tq: Combine safeguards under Article 22(5) with Parliament’s power under Article 22(7).
sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

s: The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 reduced the constitutional period for preventive detention without an Advisory Board report from three months to:
x: The 44th Amendment reduced the period from three months to two months. However, the relevant provision has not been notified, so the three-month period continues to operate.
tq: Distinguish the amended constitutional text from the provision that is actually in force.
sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

s: Why does the three-month period continue to apply to preventive detention despite the 44th Amendment?
o: The Supreme Court struck down the two-month provision
Article 22 does not contain any period relating to an Advisory Board
The amended provision was never notified
x: Although the 44th Amendment substituted two months for three months, the relevant amended clause has never been notified. Consequently, the three-month rule continues to apply.
tq: Use the implementation-status trap: distinguish an enacted amendment from a notified and operative provision.
sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

s: Which subject–legislative competence pair is correctly matched in relation to preventive detention?
o: Defence, foreign affairs and security of India — Parliament alone; public order and security of a State — Parliament and the States
Defence and foreign affairs — States alone; public order — Parliament alone
Public order — Parliament alone; security of India — States alone
Supplies essential to the community — States alone in every circumstance
x: Parliament alone legislates on preventive detention connected with defence, foreign affairs and the security of India. Parliament and the States may legislate on public order, security of a State and supplies essential to the community.
tq: Start from the sure exclusive Union subjects and then match the concurrent preventive-detention subjects.

s: Preventive detention is constitutionally justified under Article 22 in relation to which of the following?
o: Mere law and order in every local dispute
Any administrative inconvenience caused by an individual
Public order, but not merely routine law and order
Only a civil disagreement between private parties
x: The Supreme Court has distinguished public order from ordinary law and order. Preventive detention cannot be justified merely by routine law-and-order concerns.
tq: Use the higher-threshold comparison between public order and ordinary law and order.
sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

A. National Security Act

x: The Preventive Detention Act was enacted in 1950, MISA in 1971, COFEPOSA in 1974 and the National Security Act in 1980.

Its use during the Emergency and repeal in 1978
A state preventive detention law operating only in Jammu and Kashmir
A law enacted in 1980 for detention up to twelve months

s: Which preventive detention law is specifically associated with suspected smugglers and foreign-exchange manipulators?
x: The Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974, or COFEPOSA, targets suspected smugglers and foreign-exchange offenders.

It is a state law applicable only to Kerala
It was repealed in 1978 after the Emergency
It was the first preventive detention law and lapsed in 1969

Regulation III of 1818 and the Rowlatt Act

The Indian Independence Act, 1947 and the Representation of the People Act, 1951

s: Which constitutional change was introduced by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 in relation to Articles 20 and 21 during a National Emergency?
o: It made both Articles 20 and 21 unenforceable during every Emergency
It transferred the power under Article 359 from the President to the Supreme Court
It removed Article 21 from the list of Fundamental Rights
It ensured that an order under Article 359 could not suspend the enforcement of Articles 20 and 21
x: The 44th Amendment inserted the protection that the right to move courts for enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended by an order under Article 359, even during a National Emergency.
tq: Identify the amendment’s protective effect and reject the reversal that makes Articles 20 and 21 unenforceable.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Articles 20 and 21 remain enforceable during a National Emergency.
2. The protection relating to Articles 20 and 21 was inserted into Article 359 by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978.
3. The President may suspend the right to move courts for enforcement of every Fundamental Right during an Emergency.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because Article 359 does not permit suspension of the right to enforce Articles 20 and 21; its operation concerns other Fundamental Rights subject to constitutional limits.
tq: Spot the overbroad word ‘every’ in the statement about the President’s Article 359 power.
